cards.title: The Big Three
cards.author: editorial
cards.why: Provides crucial arguments and examples for International Relations papers regarding great-power diplomacy, multipolarity, and strategic stability.
cards.summary: Presidents Donald Trump, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin held an informal trilateral meeting during the APEC summit in Shenzhen. The gathering helped calm global anxiety amid ongoing conflicts in Iran and Ukraine. Crucially, the three leaders committed not to resort to nuclear weapons even in extreme adversity and endorsed United Nations reforms. The summit underscored that global politics is increasingly shifting toward multipolarity.
key_facts: The leaders of the United States, China, and Russia met informally during the APEC summit in Shenzhen.
The three leaders pledged not to use the nuclear option even under conditions of extreme adversity.
The summit produced calls for institutional reforms to the United Nations.
The leaders agreed to reduce volatility over the Strait of Hormuz and the Eurasian heartland amid simultaneous conflicts in Ukraine and Iran.

vocab.meaning: an international system where power is shared among several major states
politics based on practical and material factors rather than moral principles
generosity in spirit, attitude, or gifts

text: The Shenzhen summit of the Big Three has helped ease the nervousness prevailing amid two simultaneous wars – in Iran and Ukraine. Although no policy direction emerged from the APEC moot in the Chinese city, Presidents Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin carried the day by showing far-sightedness over realpolitik. They reportedly agreed to disagree over conflicting interests in Europe and the Middle East while stopping short of airing their concerns publicly. More reassuringly, they pledged not to exercise the nuclear option - even in extreme adversity - and called for reforms to the United Nations. The troika managed to make headlines even though they met without a formal agenda and dispersed without sowing any seeds of animosity. While the salient features of the 'peace declaration' are yet to be revealed, it seems they have agreed to lower the threshold of volatility over the Strait of Hormuz and the Eurasian heartland. That is no mean achievement, and Trump was right in saying that "we are really making history." For many, it evoked a sense of déjà vu reminiscent of Yalta 1945, where the then-victor powers sought to assert their spheres of influence while resolving not to go to war again. Shenzhen, likewise, made one thing categorically clear: the world is moving towards multipolarity. The APEC summit will long be remembered for a series of gestures that the three leaders exhibited with remarkable largesse. For the first time, Xi was seen receiving a guest at the airport - apparently as a quid pro quo for his welcome at Andrews Air Base - while Trump called Putin his "friend" and refrained from commenting on Iran. The impulsive octogenarian leader also remarked that "no peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement." That was astute diplomacy in seamless coordination. The trilateral assurance that supply chain disruptions must end brought a sigh of relief, as global production is projected to dip by 1.7 per cent. The G-3 must sustain this momentum and ensure that belligerence comes to a permanent end.

cards.title: Child rights and broken promises
cards.author: editorial
cards.why: Contains indispensable official statistics for CSS essays and Pakistan Affairs questions on human development, education, and social protection.
cards.summary: Pakistan faces a serious child rights crisis marked by pervasive labour, violence, and inadequate education. More than 8.6 million children are engaged in child labour, and over 25 million children are out of school. High rates of malnutrition leave nearly 40 percent of young children stunted, while reported sexual violence remains rampant. Although Pakistan launched the National Strategy to End Violence Against Children, implementation remains deeply deficient.
key_facts: Pakistan has roughly 120 million children, making up nearly half of the national population.
More than 8.6 million children aged 5 to 17 are in child labour, with 6.6 million engaged in hazardous work.
About four in every 10 Pakistani children under the age of five suffer from chronic stunting.
Reported sexual crimes against children reached 17,348 cases in 2025 alone.
Pakistan has over 25 million out-of-school children, the second-largest out-of-school population in the world.
The country recently introduced its first National Strategy to End Violence Against Children.

vocab.meaning: prevented from growing to normal physical size due to poor nutrition

text: World Children's Day is being observed today with the theme "My Day. My Rights. My Future", but for children in Pakistan, neither their rights nor their futures are secure. For many of the 120 million children who make up nearly half of the country's population, childhood is rarely a joyful time, and more often a nightmare fueled by deprivation, exploitation and violence. Beyond the ribbon-cuttings and events at luxury hotels, children all over the country continue to suffer due not only to the lack of several international-standard protections, but also to the abject failure to enforce most existing ones. More than 8.6 million children aged 5 to 17 are trapped in child labour, with 6.6 million confined to hazardous work that threatens their health and future. About four in every 10 children under five are stunted by chronic malnutrition. Meanwhile, up to 80 per cent of children experience violent discipline at home, while reported sexual crimes against children numbered 17,348 in 2025 alone. The numbers are so appalling that we did not even get to the fact that over 25 million children are out of school, the second-largest out-of-school population on earth. The recent launch of the first National Strategy to End Violence Against Children is a welcome acknowledgment of the crisis. But for the time being, it is just that - a strategy, and nothing more. Unless we bridge the gap between policy and implementation, millions more childhoods will be lost. But it is not just the government that is to blame. Children have been let down by society as a whole, from parents who thrash their children for sport, to community members who turn a blind eye due to cultural taboos, or religious leaders who abuse the children in their care. Some adults are lucky enough to remember the day their childhoods ended. If we can even get there, rather than forcing the harsh realities of life on our youngest citizens, it will at least be a tangible step in the right direction.
